idiom_name: pthread master loop + fixed worker threads over a mutex/condition-variable work queue
implementation_notes: C has no worker abstraction, only the primitives: pthread_create starts a worker, pthread_join is the master's join point, and a shared struct guarded by pthread_mutex plus pthread_cond_wait/pthread_cond_broadcast is the work queue. The classic structure is therefore hand-written: partition into jobs, push them under the mutex, signal one waiter per job (broadcast on shutdown), let each worker pop-and-process until it sees the done flag, then join every worker and reduce the partial results - the combine step starts only after the joins, which also order the partial-result memory. OpenMP (taskloop, which generates explicit tasks for a team and can reduce) and MPI (rank 0 as master, ranks 1..N as workers) are the library substitutes when a compiler or runtime can own the decomposition; hand-rolled pthreads remain justified for heterogeneous, long-lived or specially pinned workers, and when the queue itself is the tuning point.
pitfalls: A worker that exits on error leaves the master waiting forever: every wait needs a predicate plus an error/completion flag, so the master can tell 'no work yet' from 'worker died'.
Signalling without holding the mutex (or before a worker reaches pthread_cond_wait) loses wakeups; push and signal under the same lock and re-check the predicate in a while loop.
Broadcasting for every queued job thrashes with many workers: signal once per pushed item and reserve broadcast for shutdown, or use a work-stealing deque.
The result array is read by the master while workers may still write it: an unguarded reduction is a data race; combine only after pthread_join, which is also the synchronisation edge.
